findings.title: Self-preference inflated into divine allocation
findings.claim: The focus's assignment of sons to its hearers and females to God can be read as projecting a human value hierarchy into divine order: 16:62 names assigning to God what the speakers dislike while falsely claiming the good for themselves, whereas 42:49-50 places offspring distribution under God's will and giving.
findings.mechanism: The focus selection form activates the best-choice branch, while the linked projection and contrary-distribution passages make the asymmetry legible as a human allocation claim. The phrase describing the saying as great can consequently carry a rhetorical self-magnifying effect rather than only magnitude.
findings.reader_payoff: The utterance becomes perceptible not only as a false proposition but as a preference elevated into doctrine and presented as a statement about God's action.
findings.containment: This is a bounded rhetorical inference, not a diagnosis of individual motive. The self-magnification branch is contextual resonance, not a lexical replacement for ordinary greatness, and the linked offspring passages do not prove that the same speakers authored them.

epistemic.reason: A trusted publication supplies the bounded core reading, and exact wider target texts independently sharpen its allocation contrast; the projection mechanism remains interpretive.

findings.mechanism: 39:4 repeats the child-taking claim as a hypothetical and places choice under divine oneness; 6:139 records a distinct livestock allocation restricted by sex, while 43:19 challenges the attribution of femaleness to angels by asking for witness and accountability.
findings.reader_payoff: The female designation and the favored-son allocation become visible as a humanly imposed ordering rather than neutral classification.
findings.containment: The livestock rule is a separate practice, not the same ritual or proof of the focus claim's origin. The finding makes no universal claim about men or women; 43:19's challenge is specifically about testimony for the angel classification.

epistemic.reason: The legacy reading is narrowed to focus contacts independently supported by exact wider target text; no unbound HFT trace is treated as attribution.

findings.claim: Wider passages distinguish human assertions about offspring from choices governed by divine will and knowledge, while identifying angels among the messengers God chooses; this makes the focus's angel and offspring categories answerable to divine agency rather than human allocation.
findings.mechanism: 22:75 explicitly selects messengers from angels and people; 42:49-50 places offspring distribution under divine will, ownership, knowledge, and power; 16:74 warns against making analogies for God because God knows and humans do not.
findings.reader_payoff: The focus's contrast can be read against a wider account in which divine choosing is real but not licensed by human speculation about angelic kinship or gender.
findings.containment: Choosing messengers is not the same act as choosing offspring, and the passages do not identify angels as children. The angel branch is qualified and concerns messenger naming, not sovereignty or ownership.

epistemic.reason: Exact wider targets and focus-root branches independently ground the comparison, but the HFT source has no exact trace and the cross-context synthesis remains interpretive.
